utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. Good morning, General Galic. Madam Registrar, could you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case Number IT-98-29-T, the Prosecutor versus Stanislav Galic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I address you for one second. You will recall, Your Honour, that we did have a technical problem with a videoclip that was shown to this particular witness whom you'll be seeing first this morning. Courtesy of the good graces of my learned friends for the Defence, they would be content if we were to start today's proceedings by playing that clip again to this witness. I could ask my few questions in chief, and then my learned friend Ms. Pilipovic would be prepared to carry on her cross-examination. If that suits your schedule for the way things should proceed, Your Honour, I would suggest that's how we should do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If that's the order you managed to agree upon, I'm only glad to do it as you wish. So that means that -- unless -- I see Mr. Piletta-Zanin is asking for the floor. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, thank you to give me the floor, Mr. President. We have indeed agreed 30 seconds ago with Mr. Blaxill that the video could be played again before any statement by the Defence. But Mr. Blaxill, I don't think you have indicated to me that you would ask questions immediately. Therefore, it is not reasonable I think, to interrupt a cross-examination, to insert questions of the Prosecution. We agreed to play the video, Mr. Blaxill, but I don't think I heard you say to the Defence that you could ask questions immediately after. So our agreement doesn't stand, is broken as from now.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Your Honours, I -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I was too optimistic a couple of minutes ago that you had agreed upon something. The video will be played, that's the decision of the Court, after the cross-examination has been completed. So Ms. Pilipovic, you may proceed, once the witness has been brought in, with the cross-examination. Could you please bring in the witness, Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Mandilovic -- Dr. Mandilovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I understand that you can hear me in a language you understand. May I remind you that you are still bound by the solemn declaration you made at the beginning of your testimony, and the Defence may now proceed the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Mandilovic.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: On Friday, at the end of our working day, we were discussing the question of whether on the 2nd of May you were at your workplace.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, on 2nd of May, I had left the hospital. Actually, I had left my workplace.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When was that? What time?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in the morning hours, before noon. I think it was a Saturday, actually, but I'm not quite sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You live in the Novi Grad municipality?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, in the Novo Sarajevo municipality

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Oh, I see. I apologise. How did you go to work from your home to your workplace, and how long did it take to you get to work?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Usually, I would walk, which meant that it took me 25 minutes to half an hour, or I took the tram, or I went in my own car.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: On that particular day, how did you go?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That day, I went by tram.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you happen to know that on that particular day, there was something going on in town, something special? Were there any incidents or anything out of the ordinary?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally did not see any incidents taking place, but later on, during the afternoon and evening, from the media, because it was the time when the media was active, there was electricity, and you could follow programmes, there were -- I learned that there had indeed been incidents in town. And I think that the tram transport was stopped later on. I had already reached my home by that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Who were the parties to the incident? Do you happen to know?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The incident was between some structures of the Yugoslav people's army and the members of the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you happen to know that on that particular day, there were casualties, that persons taking part in the incident were wounded and injured?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was something like that. But I couldn't tell you exactly the number of the casualties or what actually happened. I really can't say.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You are a major by rank?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was a major.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: That means you were a higher officer. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did you learn that your fellow officers and noncommissioned officers were injured and wounded on that day as well?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that there was an incident that took place that day when a group of soldiers, a small group of soldiers, started out from the military hospital, which is where they were stationed, and that they moved in a direction of the headquarters of the 2nd military district to help out a situation with a truck. And there was an incident that took place in the Vojvode Stepe Street, which is the right bank of the Mijecka River, and some people were injured and I think some were killed as well, but I can't tell you any figures today with any certainty.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You said that a couple of soldiers from the military hospital were concerned.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: What day was that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you about when they left the military hospital.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that was the 2nd of May. I didn't see it actually happen, but from the media as it was reconstructed, I think that it was the 2nd of May. And that small contingent of soldiers, I think there were 10 to 15 of them, they were led by an officer, I think he was captain first class by rank or a younger officer was stationed -- a noncommissioned officer was stationed in the building of the military hospital from approximately mid-April.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: What floor were they on?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were on the 12th floor, and later on, after my departure, they cleared out the 12th floor, and the 11th floor as well, and that's where they were put up.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Let me remind you that yesterday, or rather on Friday, in response to a question by my learned friend, Mr. Blaxill, when asked whether in the military hospital there was any -- there were any soldiers, you said there were not, and that you had never seen them in hospital. You had never seen any military presence in the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. I thought the question related to the period after the Yugoslav people's army units had left the military hospital, and I apologise if you misunderstood me or if I misunderstood. May I just complete my answer, please. After the 10th of May, actually, in the military or the newly named state hospital, there were no -- there was no more military presence.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When I started my cross-examination, my question for you was the following: Whether, in the hospital --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I just wonder if my learned friend could give us a page reference in the transcript she is referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't know whether they have available already, Ms. Pilipovic, the transcript. I did not receive yet a transcript this morning, so I don't know whether it will be possible to have the transcript on the screen. Unfortunately, I'm afraid that we can't do it at this moment. Usually, we have it available the next morning, but since we switched from afternoon session to morning sessions, we haven't.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I believe we have Livenote on the computer, on the laptop.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't know if you can scroll back to an earlier day. You can?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I can give you the time. It was 18.09 hours, to be exact, 35. 18.09, I made a note of it. I haven't got the official version of the transcript, but the time was 18.09, 35.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I suggest that the Registry will try to look into the transcript of last Friday at the time mentioned by the Defence, or if you have got it available... I think we need some patience, but the Registrar is really trying hard. May I ask the Defence, the time you indicated, was this the time from the big screen or on the laptop computer? Because there's a time difference of approximately 11 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Laptop, 18.09.35.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What's the best way to proceed, Madam Registrar? Can we either have a printout of a few lines, then I can read them, or we could invite the Defence could read the specific part?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am trying to find on the diskette of Friday those elements. If I find them immediately, I'll let you know, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think Madam Registrar is already printing the... It's Monday morning, not only the parties but also the printer needs warming up. Perhaps would it be possible for you to proceed and come back to this question later, once we have the printout of that part of the transcript. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: On that 2nd of May, you say that over the media, you learned of an incident that took place between the army and, as you said, the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: According to your knowledge, how many officers were wounded on that occasion, how many noncommissioned officers and how many soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said a moment ago that I know for certain that some were killed, but one officer was killed and I think one soldier as well and that several others were wounded, but I really don't know the exact number. I apologise. I can't tell you any figures.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You are a member of the medical corps of the JNA. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: And your number was 32509. Was that right? What were you, as a member of the medical corps and as a doctor yourself; what did you do? What measures did you take to help in -- to help your colleagues out and also the citizens who were casualties? Which military post did you report to?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After I left the military hospital, I did not report to any military post. I reported to the local community.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When did you leave the military post?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 2nd of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Who did you report your departure to?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The head of the military hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Who was the head of the military hospital at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Doctor Tomislav Tausan.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did you report to him in writing or orally?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Orally.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did you tell him why you were leaving?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: And what was the reason for your departure? What reason did you give him?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that it was because at that particular time, the units of the Yugoslav people's army were no longer a regular military force. In view of the fact that the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina had been recognised on the east river, then the Territorial Defence became the regular military force of that particular state. And the police or the reserve police becomes its security force by the same token.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You said that the JNA was a professional army?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: By rank, you are a high-ranking officer, a higher ranking officer. May I correct... Your father was a military man as well. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: How do you explain the way in which you departed from the army or how you left your military post at a point in time when incidents were taking place and when the Yugoslav army, the Yugoslav people's army, was being attacked as you, yourself, said both in Slovenia and in Croatia, and according to you, this was happening in Sarajevo, too, because you said yesterday when I was questioning you that the patriotic league had, in fact, surrounded the hospital? You never made mention at all that there was any army in the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You didn't ask me. You didn't ask me about the army. I apologise. You didn't ask me, and that was the way in which your examination ran, that you never reached that question, and I didn't want to jump the gun, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: But I asked you whether it was -- whether the statement you gave to the investigators of the Tribunal was true where you said that the patriotic league had surrounded the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's like this: Just a minute.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please slow down. Make pauses between question and answer, please.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I answer? It was like this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, there was a question - I don't know whether it has been translated for you - to make a pause between the answer given and the new question to be put to the witness because it goes too quick, as we experienced before. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you answer my question, please?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Would you repeat your question?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did the patriotic league surround the hospital and which were the forces of the patriotic league?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I say "patriotic league," I mean the patriotic forces or the patriotic front. And with that term, I also mean the regular forces of the newly established state of Bosnia-Herzegovina. This implies the Territorial Defence, the police, and the reserve police force, too.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So the patriotic league was not the Territorial Defence; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The patriotic league, in a word, is patriotic. They are patriotic forces, the patriotic front. All that makes up the patriotic league.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Which forces made up that patriotic league?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just said the Territorial Defence and the police force.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When the patriotic forces surrounded the military hospital, where were you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I should like to mention one point.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you where were you. It's a short question. Where were Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I just take a little time to expand upon that? I don't think it was a classical form of encirclement.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my question was merely where the witness was at that particular time when the patriotic league had formed a circle around the hospital. I don't think we should waste time.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: My question is very short, a short one: Where were you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot answer your question because the question is a very sharp one. You're talking about an encirclement. I don't think it was a classical encirclement or siege. It was more a matter of control.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I asked you where you were when the patriotic forces surrounded the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in the hospital, and later on I was outside the hospital because it's an hour, this whole process went on for an hour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: How long did the process go on for?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it lasted until the Yugoslav people's army left the premises of the military hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: How long did that last, how many days?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The military hospital, or rather the forces of the Yugoslav people's army left the military hospital, I think, on the 10th of May. I think a month, and then the patriotic forces controlled the hospital and the area around it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So you'll agree with me that the members of the patriotic forces for one month controlled the surroundings of the hospital and provided security for the hospital. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say that was the time it was, but other people might be able to give you more exact information.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Were they armed? I mean the members of the patriotic forces.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only saw the police section of the patriotic forces, and they had light weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Were they present inside the hospital as well?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: After, as you yourself said, the agreement, and that, according to you, was on the 10th of May?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure it was the 10th of May because the 10th of May was the time of departure from the hospital. I think it was one or two days prior to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell me exactly when?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know. I wasn't in the hospital at that time. I only learned this from the media so I wasn't in the hospital actually, but I think that that was on the 7th or 8th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Blaxill.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: If I could just interpose and ask if my learned friend could explain the relevancy of all this detail of a period that well pre-dates the indictment period. I know we've had to deal with some elements of background to the conflict, I think that's appropriate, but at this point my learned friend does seem to be dwelling in enormous detail on something which I am now questioning the relevance of this direction in such detail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, could you please explain the relevance of this questioning in detail on this subject.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, before the witness started answering questions in the cross-examination by the Defence, I asked the witness whether he had made a statement to the investigators of the Tribunal on the 11th of February, 2000. The witness asserted that he did, in fact, make a statement. The witness statement is six pages long. After that, I asked him whether he had a talk with the Tribunal's investigators, and that was in September and on the 2nd of October. And the witness said "yes" to that. My cross-examination and my testing of the credibility of the witness moves within this framework, that is to say, the examination-in-chief by my learned colleague and within the frameworks of the statements given to the investigators of the Tribunal. And the Defence has these statements, having been given them by my learned colleagues. My second point is the following: I'm going to tell you that the witness yesterday spoke about, in answer to my colleague's friends, that at the beginning of the conflict, which broke out in 1992, and the incidents that took place, and particularly the incident when the barracks was surrounded, he answered those questions. Now, my question refers to May because the witness talked about that. I just want to test whether he's telling the truth. Had my learned colleagues limited their examination-in-chief to the relevant period in the indictment, then my cross-examination would be within that relevant period of the indictment as well. But in view of the fact that the witness was questioned from the beginning of 1992, about events from the beginning of 1992, and then it went on through 1993 and 1994, it is precisely for these reasons that the Defence in its cross-examination wishes to test the credibility of this witness and to ascertain in simple terms whether the witness is telling the truth, both in his statements and in response to the questions he is being asked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think you're right to the extent that the examination-in-chief also covered this period of time. On the other hand, I can imagine that some details are, even for the credibility of the witness, are not of that major importance, so perhaps if you could concentrate on those issues that really matter in the -- in the questioning, then perhaps we could proceed a bit more quickly. I remind that you, for example, on some issues in earlier cross-examination you asked on every single place whether the witness was aware of the exact lines, the exact positions of the armies. And the answer was again, no, no, no. Perhaps if you could try to first find out whether the witness has some relevant knowledge in general on certain issues, and then perhaps go in more detail if it turns out he has. The only reason I'm telling you this, I see the relevance of your questioning. On the other hand, I think if you could do it just as efficient as possible so that we don't lose too much time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have to state the position that was agreed between the Prosecution and the Defence, and that is that the cross-examination may last as long as the examination-in-chief. I will try to keep my cross-examination within this duration, and not cross the limit. My question, to what extent the patriotic league was present, for how long, the witness answered, for a month. And I asked him where he got this information. That was his own answer. If he had said I don't know. I wouldn't have had any more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Blaxill.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Just a point on which I would correct my learned friend. It wasn't an issue of agreement between the parties that any cross-examination be limited in time to the examination-in-chief time. That was contents of the order of 16th November from the learned Pre-Trial Judge, and it is a matter which is currently under appeal. So it wasn't a matter of agreement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do agree with you it was not part of the order, as far as I remember, but it was part of the suggestion made by the Pre-Trial Chamber. There's still an appeal pending. Let me just say this: Even if you would agree that cross-examination should take perhaps not more time than the examination-in-chief, this doesn't say that it must take the same time. So the only question at this moment is do it as efficient as possible. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I thank my learned friend. It is indeed the decision on the 16th November by the Pre-Trial Judge, Judge Rodriguez.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: From the 2nd of May, 1992 until when didn't you come to your workplace?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think until the 12th of May, I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When was your employment with the JNA terminated?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 2nd of May.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You stated that the army of Republika Srpska grew out of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Will you agree with me that the Yugoslav people's army divided along ethnic lines?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That it divided along ethnic lines? That it split along ethnic lines? Was that your question?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in principle, yes, with the departure of Slovenia, of Croatia, of Macedonia, there occurred a rift in the Yugoslav People's army which could no longer have this attribute, peoples.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You said that the command corps of the Republika Srpska was made of the command corps of the former JNA?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's my opinion, yes. Basically, I don't claim that all the officers transferred, nor do I know the majority of them. But it is certain that there was a cadre of the former JNA. They were present in all armies.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You say in all armies. Which armies do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean the army of Republic of Slovenia, the army of the Republic of Croatia, certainly in the army of Republika Srpska, and in the newly-established army, that is, the Territorial Defence of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When did you start working in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have said this already. On the 12th or the 13th of May.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When were the first patients brought in with injuries inflicted by firearms from the time when you began working? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm trying to remember. I'm trying to be as precise as I can because it has been a long time, really. It was a continuous process, and it's only a question of number, just a few days after my -- after I started working at the hospital, patients started coming in in large numbers. I remember that there was constant -- there was a constant inflow of regular patients with chronic conditions, more or less usual conditions. The hospital never stopped working.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Were there more civilians or soldiers at the hospital then?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Civilians.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Were there any soldiers of the JNA at your hospital?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were soldiers of the JNA who had been left behind, who had been in treatment before, and their treatment had not been completed so they had to remain in the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did you treat them?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge that there were colleagues of yours who refused to treat members of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that there were no such doctors at the state hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You said that there were more civilians than soldiers in that initial period. Will you please specify what period that was when you had -- when you got your first soldiers along with civilians at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me get one thing straight: Whose soldiers do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You said there were soldiers and civilians among the patients.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but whose soldiers, soldiers of the JNA or soldiers of the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I asked you first were there civilians and soldiers, and then I asked you whether there were soldiers of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I was precise enough. There were soldiers whose treatment required a longer time, and regardless of the fact that the JNA had left the hospital, they remained at the hospital continuing their treatment. And they were treated in a completely normal way, regardless of the political environment.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Were there any soldiers of the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That was probably already towards the end of May and the beginning of June.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: During admission of patients to the hospital, in what way did you make records of their admission, and did you record the fact they were soldiers or civilians?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is an admissions record, a protocol, where you record the name, surname, name of father, the year of birth, and status.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you want to explain what "status" means?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether it's a soldier or a civilian.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So you wrote in your protocol "civilian" or "soldier"; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If the person is civilian, you would write that he is a civilian. If he is a soldier, you would write that he is a soldier.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, you have to do that. How would we know the next day or after so many years, how would we be able to preserve the records of our former patients?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: All those soldiers who were admitted by you, were they dressed in uniform, and what did those uniforms look like?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, members of the Territorial Defence did not have any uniforms in the initial stage. They wore mostly their own clothes, civilian clothes, or alternatively, they wore parts of uniforms. Members of the police did have their own uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: What does it mean if the protocol explicitly states "civilian" or "soldier," how is such a patient treated, or how do you think --

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are asking if there is no such specification, if it is not explicitly stated.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: If somebody simply fails to write in "civilian" or "soldier"?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There can be no such failure. You have to write something. Alongside the year of birth, you have to write "civilian" or "soldier."

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: That's what I wanted you to confirm. So it was not possible to leave this column blank?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You said yesterday -- I mean the last time when you were questioned by my learned friend, that the hospital was on the separation line, on the demarcation line, just a hundred metres away from the confrontation line, or 300 to 400 metres as the crow flies?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I think I put it this way: The position of the hospital on Marijin Dvor was about 300 to 400 metres away from the right bank of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the Mijecka River, and the Mijecka River was practically the separation line.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: The separation line between whom and whom?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The forces of the Territorial Defence and the forces of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me, between those parties to the confrontation, was there any fighting?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: How frequent was the fighting?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was very frequent. That is to say, the shelling was very frequent. As for direct combat, I can't say because I was not on the front line. But the shelling was constant.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: In relation to the separation line which was the Mijecka River, where were the positions of the BH army?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the logic of things, they were along the Mijecka River.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: What facilities are located there? You said on the right bank, along the right bank, so which side was it, north, east?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We are talking about the south side relative to the hospital, because both the Mijecka River and the Grbavica mountain was on the south side. And you see the right bank when you look from the source to the confluence, which means that it was the bank closer to the hospital. That was the right bank.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Where were the positions of the BH army if you look at this right bank of the Mijecka River in juxtaposition to the hospital? Could you specify their positions?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think one of their positions was -- at least what we could see from the hospital, I think the most prominent position of their defences was the building of the BH parliament.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: That building of the parliament, does it shield the building of the hospital?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it is far from the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Looking towards the Mijecka River, towards the right bank?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is right next to the right bank of the Mijecka River.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: What other buildings are there?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The building of the philosophical faculty, the building of the geographical museum, the building of the mechanical engineering faculty. There are also residential buildings, empty lots, the building of the electrical company and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Where were the soldiers and the troops located, those who were on the right side of the separation line, in juxtaposition to the Mijecka River?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I never inspected those lines or positions, never during the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Relative to the east, as viewed from the hospital. We now talked about the south side and the existence of the separation line along the Mijecka River. You told us about the buildings, the high-rise buildings alongside the Mijecka River.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, there is no high-rise building which would shield the hospital or block the view of the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: How tall were the buildings?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The building of the parliament is rather low in height, and then there is another building which is high-rise, but it is -- its position is such that it's not directly opposite, so it cannot block the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Viewed from this south side, looking at the right bank of the Mijecka where the separation line was, from those positions where the line was, was there any fighting relative to the other bank of the River?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see any fighting, no traditional infantry fighting. There was only shelling that I can note.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: But in answer to my question, you said there was fighting between the two warring parties, and those were the Territorial Defence and the army of the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were confronted, but as for traditional infantry fighting, I heard the sound of infantry weapons. I heard a wide range of noise from artillery weapons, but I never saw any traditional infantry fighting or battle because that was too far away.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You said you saw the shelling or you heard it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard the shelling. And then, you see, shelling has one feature, if the piece firing the shell is above you, you see a glow at a certain point, and a couple of moments later, you hear the detonation, whereas with infantry weapons, you cannot see it because you don't know where it is unless it's very close by.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did you see the shell or did you just hear the explosion?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, the war was a very protracted one and the shelling lasted for a long time. And there were certainly occasions when we could see, when we could observe the shelling that -- we could directly see the glow, the blasts from the pieces and then hear the sounds.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: How did you watch that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We observed it for the entire duration of the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Specifically, would you please describe one or two incidents that you observed where the shells fell and what they damaged?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. You see, as far as the town is concerned, I have no direct knowledge. I have only indirect knowledge from the patients who came in, and from the media. As for direct observations, I can tell you about the hits that the hospital took on the south side.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The hospital was hit many times on the south side from the beginning of the war until 1995, until the Dayton Accord. It's very difficult to name the figure now, but there were many hits.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did you see any instances of those -- this shelling of the hospital?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. At one point, I was on the same floor that was hit by a shell.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When was that and what was damaged on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was on the 11th floor, in the corridor, and suddenly I hear a huge impact. The whole framework of the building began to tremble. Then I heard a huge acoustic impact, then a blast, then a lot of dust, laboured restoration and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did you see that shell coming and falling on the 11th floor or did you just hear it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't see it. I don't think you can see it at all. I was just present on that location when this mortar or artillery shell -- you cannot really distinguish in that tumult of noises what it was. I was present there about 10 metres away from the room which was hit and completely destroyed by the shell. And not only that room, but also two neighbouring rooms and a part of the corridor.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: How far is the Marsal Tito barracks from the hospital?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's about 400, 500 metres away.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who was inside the Marsal Tito barracks?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were members of the Yugoslav people's army housed in the Marsal Tito barracks, and students of the military school until a certain point when they left, and I can't tell you the date. They were relocated.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: After the relocation, who was inside the barracks?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was the forces of the UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: How far is the railway station from the hospital?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: About the same distance, 500, 600 metres.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You have already explained to us if we can call it the south line of separation to the south relative to the Mijecka River. Where is the separation line on the east?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the east, it is along the suburbs of the Stari Grad municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: How far is that from the hospital?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean as the crow flies or by road?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You can tell me both if you know.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know by road, but it's certainly several kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Relative to the east, where were the positions of the BH army and where were the positions of the Republika Srpska army?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: In that section, was there any fighting between the warring parties?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There probably was because there was shelling and certainly if there is shelling, then there is probably a certain amount of fighting. I, however, haven't seen infantry fighting. It's too far away, for one, and secondly, I was never in that area.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Will you explain to us the positions relative to the north side and the northeast of the hospital?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the positions of the VRS was somewhere on Polina [phoen]. You can see it from the upper floors of the hospital if you look to the north. But where exactly the line was, I don't know. But that is, if I may call it, the northern destination.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Where were the positions of the BH army?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. In front of them, probably.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Was there any damage to the north side of the hospital?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. But to a smaller extent than on the south side, far smaller.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you explain to us the western side of the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The west is the narrow portion of the hospital, and the western side, or rather when you get to the western balcony and western side of the hospital, your view is towards parts of Grbavica and Vrace, and you can also see Ilidza and Rajlovac, so that's that western side moving from the southwest to the west.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Now, on this western side, westerly reaches of the hospital, the hospital looks towards the Grbavica settlement. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the hospital and Grbavica settlement are placed parallel, but this western side, when you get to the western side actually, you can see the Grbavica area but you can also see Ilidza, Rajlovac, and a whole spectrum. You have a whole broad angle of vision from that western side, from the southwest to the northwest, so it's not just one side and one area. It's a broad angle of vision.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Is the Grbavica settlement -- does it border on to the Hrasno settlement? Is there a square in between?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: And from the southern side, can you see the Hrasno settlement?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which southern side?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: The hospital side. I mean, can you see Hrasno?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you can partially, in part, not very well. You can say Hrasno is over there, but you can't see it clearly because it's at a great distance.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you happen to know which inhabitants lived in the Grbavica municipality -- rather, the Grbavica settlement or the Hrasno? Were there any positions there, if you happen to know or not?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're asking me about the composition of the population, you mean ethnically?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, ethnically speaking.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I know is the following: I wasn't there at the time during the war, but I do know that the inhabitants of Grbavica was predominantly Serbs. Predominantly, not exclusively, though.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: What about the Hrasno settlement?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Hrasno settlement was predominantly inhabited by the Bosniaks, predominantly, but let me say that the entire area, the part of Sarajevo which was under the control, for all practical purposes, of the Territorial Defence was a multi-ethnic population.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You said that the shelling of the hospital, that you saw the shelling of the 11th floor of the hospital, in fact, that you were on the 11th floor?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was there in person. On that occasion, when the shelling took place, rather, I was in the vicinity. But that kind of shelling was very frequent during the war. I was lucky just to be near the shelling on that one occasion. Or the other occasions when the projectiles hit the hospital, I was on the lower floors or in the theatre, operations theatre, so that the -- apart from the trembling that I felt caused by the detonations, by the explosions, there were no other consequences for me.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So don't know what that month was?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about the shelling of the 11th floor.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was sometime in 1993, but exactly when, I really can't say -- I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Where is the Kosovo tunnel in relation to the hospital and how far away is it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which Kosovo tunnel do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I mean the Ciglane settlement.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In relation to the hospital, I would say the Ciglane settlement was behind the hospital to the northern side, and I'm sure it must be, as the crow flies, a kilometre or one and a half kilometres in a straight line. But from the hospital, you can't see the Ciglane settlement or the tunnel because there's a hill that rises up behind the hospital which blocks your view towards that settlement.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: What hill is that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know what the name is. A nameless hill. It's an elevation, actually.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Were there any military objects on that hill?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not see any.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: In relation to the hospital, where was the UNIS building located?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The UNIS building is -- there were two buildings in fact.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. There were two high-rise buildings.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In relation to the hospital, they are precisely to the southwest.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: How far away as the crow flies would you say?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Several hundred metres.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you happen to know that there were sniper nests on those two buildings throughout the duration of the conflict?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I didn't see them. I didn't see anybody or anything. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: What about over the media? Did you hear that somebody had been hit from those spots? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: What about the Electroprijedor building?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the Electroprijedor building, I know from the media that, just like on the parliamentary building, there were the Territorial Defence members because there is a bridge next to that building, then to the left of the parliament is a bridge and to the left of the Electroprijedor buildings there was the bridge, and these were bridges that were -- for which security was provided. You have the Mijecka River flowing underneath them so that quite naturally, that was there.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You said that the shelling of Sarajevo took place during the night as well?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it did take place during the night as well, although percentage-wise I think that the daily shellings were more intensive than the ones that took place during the night.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Was the hospital shelled at night?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember any night-time hits. I really can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Were there cases when civilians were wounded in front of the hospital?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were. There were.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: During the conflict, was security provided for the hospital?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Who provided the hospital security?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The forces of the reserve police force, and that was only at the gate, at the entrance gate.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You have told us that the hospital was damaged mostly by artillery fire.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't make an assessment of that, really. The hospital -- perhaps I could put it this way and explain it in this way. Along the facades, particularly the western, southerly, and eastern facades, the facades were damaged by artillery fire, but some hits created much greater damage. Infantry fire created much greater damage.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: The shells, the results of the shells hitting the building, is that visible? Can they be seen?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they can.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Were parts of the walls so damaged that the floors were not able to function, that nothing on that particular floor was able to function?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The entire southern side was not operational. The whole southern side of the hospital, wing of the hospital, was not operational throughout the war. And all the activities had to be transferred to the northern side, and during the intensive shelling phases, everything was transferred to the lower floors.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: During the conflict, were some floors completely out of order, if I can put it that way, not working?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. The upper stories were not operational at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Which upper floors?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the 12th floor to the 5th floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: They weren't working at all, you couldn't use them at all. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's like this: The northern wing was used, but because of the intensive shelling, you couldn't use it properly. When the intensity of the shelling subsided, then the activities of the hospital would move upwards, the floors above. When the shelling was intensive, all the hospital's activities would go down to the lower floors. So you can't say that throughout the whole floor, all the floors were not operational. The northern wing did work, was open. It just depended on the stage and intensity of the shelling as to how much those floors and that wing was used.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did journalists visit the hospital?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When did these visits take place?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Throughout the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Were the journalists put up, accommodated in the hospital somewhere, or did they just come and go, come for short visits? Or did they stay in the hospital for a day or two? How long did they stay?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, in the first stage, that is to say, the end of May, the journalists who visited the hospital would tour the hospital, and then they would actually stay in the hospital for a day or two. But later on, after June, they found some other places to stay in town so that they would just make their visits that lasted several hours, and then leave.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You said that the shelling came from the direction of Vrace, Trebevic, and the Jewish cemetery?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You also said that the Jewish cemetery itself was located on the southern side, south of the hospital, under Mount Trebevic, if I recall?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. The Jewish cemetery is at a small elevation, and they are the slopes -- it's the beginning of the slopes of Mount Trebevic, and it's opposite the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you happen to know where the Osmice Motel is located on that side?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Osmice Motel is far higher up, and more northerly or northeasterly, and it is on Mount Trebevic itself. It's quite a long way off from there to the Jewish cemetery. It's also on the south side, but viewed exactly from the hospital, it would be more to the southeastern side.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you happen to know that during the conflict that was where the BH army positions were?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I mean under the Osmice Motel

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, but quite possibly, they were.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: In respect to the southern side of the hospital, viewed from that side, can you see some hills at the foot of Mount Trebevic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean from the south side?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. What can you see?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can see the whole of Trebevic. If you were able to go up to the top floors, if you dared go up to the top floors and look through the open windows and the destroyed windows, the shattered glass, then you could see Mount Trebevic in front of you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You were a military man yourself?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You said you attended military training sessions?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: And you said you were in the medical corps and you had a military post?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did you go to do training and exercises at Debelo Brdo?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember ever going there.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: And where in respect to the south side of the hospital was Debelo Brdo?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the southern side of the hospital?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know where Debelo Brdo is. I don't know where it lies because there are lots of hills around Sarajevo. Now Debelo Hill or Debelo Brdo is something I'm not acquainted with.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: What about Colina Kapa, have you heard about that Colina Kapa, Velika and Mala --

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Colina Kapa is at Trebevic. It's a long way off from the hospital towards the northeast.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you happen to know who controlled positions at Colina Kapa, which is at the foot of Trebevic, as you said a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Either the Territorial Defence or the Territorial Defence and the army of Republika Srpska. I really don't know where that border line was. You couldn't see that at all, however hard you looked.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Were you ever at Colina Kapa?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I mean, you say you can't see it so how do you know?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I -- you can't see it from the hospital. I was never there but I couldn't see the demarcation line.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You have said that there was a lot of shelling. Can you tell us for 1992, 1993, and 1994, what the intensity was looking at those years?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, the most intensive shelling took place in the second half of 1992, in 1993. And after 1993, the shelling slowly subsided. In 1994, there were periods where there was a lull, and peaceful periods established by the international community. And how long this went on for, I can't say. But the best answer, to the best of my recollection, is that the highest intensity was in 1992 and 1993, and during 1994 and 1995, the shelling subsided. Looking at the situation as a whole, of course this does not mean that there were not a great many casualties in the latter half. The shelling might have been less frequent, but their destructive power was still very great.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, whether the hospital was visited by members of UNPROFOR and UN observers?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did you talk to them?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not me, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you happen to know who contacted them on behalf of the hospital?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the management of the hospital, rather, the state hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: More specifically, who from the management, any specific person or the whole management team?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that stage, we did not have a port parole for public relations. We didn't have a public relations man, so it must have been the whole of the management team. But the most exposed person when it came to these guests was the executive director of the hospital itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: And who was the executive director?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was Dr. Bakir Nakas.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When these incidents took place, and let me quote an example in point, the one on the 11th floor where you yourself were present, who did you inform about the incident that took place, and did anybody come, any representative of the official bodies, to take note of the situation, take stock of it and to look at the -- what was caused by the incident?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, I informed the administration. But they were such onslaughts which were so visible that you didn't have to report specifically. Anybody who happened to be in the hospital at that time was conscious of a projectile having hit the hospital. The only thing that you couldn't know was where the hospital had been hit, actually. It was such a strong explosion and so shattering that there was absolutely no dilemma whether it was a hit or not, but yes, we did inform the administration, and then they would take the necessary steps and look at the extent of the damages, appraise, assess the extent of the damage.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who would come on the spot to perform this examination?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The members of the management would.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did any representative of the government of the authorities or UN observers and UNPROFOR come?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember an event of that kind, but quite possibly they did.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Regardless of the fact that you yourself were not a member of the management at that level, was the question of the hospital's work and functioning resolved, because you said that the regular lines were between 100 and 300 metres?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, only at that level.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Were you present when those meetings took place?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I attended professional meetings, but not the management meetings concerning administration.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: But you do know that such meetings were held?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean administration managerial meetings? Well, they must have been, otherwise, how could you manage such a large institution? Quite certainly, there were.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you happen to know whether any solutions were found to the work and functioning of the hospital as it was located along the separation line, 100 to 300 metres as the crow flies?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, 100 metres would be too close. But 300 or 400 metres, yes, that would be right, that would be the distance. And the characteristic feature, and I would like to stress this, was that the hospital, during the war, did not stop working for a single second. There was nobody who was wounded and injured today who would say that he did not get adequate medical assistance in the hospital at that time. Everybody did, and I think that the management was responsible for that, through their own personal initiative and work, enabled the continuous functioning of the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So you don't know of any meeting or protest on the part of the management with respect to the hospital's position in view of the fact - let me repeat again - that throughout the war the hospital was working only 300 to 400 metres away from the separation line, from the front line?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no choice. It had to go on working.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you happen to know that some hospitals from Sarajevo were displaced, and that in the surrounds of Sarajevo, field hospitals or provisional hospitals were set up?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that, but quite possibly the Territorial Defence did set up their infirmaries or field hospitals, because that is the principle of every modern-day army.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you happen to know where the inhabitants of Grbavica went for treatment if they had any health problems or if they were injured or wounded?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think -- I can only say that on the basis of what I heard, if you accept that, if you accept that kind of statement. But I didn't see it myself. But I do know that later on, that at Grbavica, there was a general practice dispensary, an infirmary, and the army of Republika Sprska had its own. There was a military hospital at Sokolac, and another hospital set up at Pale, and in Kasindol, there was a hospital there, too which in peacetime had been a hospital for chest diseases, lung diseases. And I think those were the health institutions of the Serb population or, rather, the army of Republika Srpska but I did not visit them during the war. I'm just telling you that from what my colleagues told me and from what I learned from the media.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: How about Ilidza, was there a hospital there during the conflict?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't hear about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Where did the inhabitants of Ilidza, Vogosca, go for treatment, and those settlements?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know. Probably, they had dispensaries or infirmaries, outpatient departments of some kind there.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You said that the Grbavica inhabitants went for treatment to the hospitals that you mentioned where the Serbs would get medical treatment. So that would mean that the hospital you worked in treated the Muslim ethnic population group?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not what I said. You asked me where the inhabitants of Grbavica went for medical treatment, and I said -- I answered your question on the basis of the knowledge I had received from the media and others. But the overall population was treated in the health institutions which were under the control of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that was a multi-ethnic population. I have to say that. It was a multi-ethnic population, which means in our hospital during the war, we gave medical treatment to members of all ethnic groups, and you can see that from our protocol books.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did you make entries in your protocol book and write in the nationalities, Serb, Croat, and so on? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we did not. No.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So how then can you see this from the ethnic makeup, from the protocol book?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you know our names are usually quite specific, so by looking at a name, for all practical purposes in the majority of cases, you can judge the ethnic affiliation of a person on the basis of their name. Not always, of course, but usually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, may I ask you, looking at the clock, it's almost 10.30. How much time would you still need to conclude your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, you would like us to take a break. I think I will need another 10 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then perhaps I suggest that you try to do it as quick as possible, and you finish it first, if that's okay with the interpreters. So if you take another 10 minutes, that would be an hour and a half.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said an hour and a half, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay, we'll look in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think I said an hour and a half, Your Honour. At the end of the transcript, I think you will find it. But I will adhere to the 10-minute time limit now.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You have told us that occasionally, there was water available. Can you tell us what the situation was with gas at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, occasionally we had water. That's true. And as for gas, we were connected to the gas pipeline later, and the supply was irregular.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Since you mentioned that the hospital had its own generators, electricity generators, were they working?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were, but they are only small appliances, small generators which provide electricity to operating theatres and enable complex technological equipment to work, whereas the big generator was never switched on because it consumes a lot of oil.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: As for humanitarian aid, from which organisations did you receive it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about organisations. We received it from the international community, generally speaking.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You told us that the aid was bad, that the medication was of bad quality. What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We cannot generalise here, nor should we. Out of the aid contingents that we received, there was a wide range of medical supplies, including some whose date of expiry was past, including some inadequate pharmaceuticals.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: What does it mean, inadequate medicine?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That means when you get medicine against malaria while you are in the town of Sarajevo. An inadequate medicine is a medicine which is intended for a totally different area. Generally speaking, this aid was never the best in terms of adequacy and sufficiency, but it was good.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have any problems with oxygen supply?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did have major problems with that. And at one stage, we were helped out by the UNPROFOR who brought us oxygen bottles. And later on, we managed to procure, again through the international community, oxygenators or oxygen generators, and for the first time we started performing operations, providing anaesthesia with the help of these supplies.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Who was in charge of oxygen supplies in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I really don't know. You have to ask the management. At any rate, it was the technical service.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Were there any problems with the issuing of oxygen? Did the oxygen bottles disappear?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I think not.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: And another question, you told us that you wrote in the admissions protocol whether a person was a civilian or a soldier.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You told us that Serbs were treated at the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said the Serbs, too. Of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that Serbs who had been brought from the prison were treated at the hospital, people with visible injuries from physical mistreatment and beating?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no knowledge about that at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, those would be all my questions, with the proviso that I would like to ask this witness additional questions if my learned friends from the Prosecution are allowed further questioning about the video material that will be shown later. I would prefer to wait for my colleagues from the Prosecution to ask their questions about the videoclip, and then I would have some additional questions regarding their examination on the video material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will consider that during the break, Ms. Pilipovic. I have, however, to point out to you that when the Prosecution asked to question immediately upon showing the video, your co-counsel said that it was not agreed that they could immediately put any questions. So we will consider that during the break. I've got one more question to you at this moment. We had some difficulties in the beginning to find the exact place in the transcript on the presence of military in the hospital. Has this been clarified by now, and would this cause any additional question to be put to the witness at this moment? Because we have still 3 or 4 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
