utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to have the official result. I said it was 18.09.35. And if we could have the question read out from the transcript, I would appreciate it. Whether it was a question concerning the presence of military units, that is, if there were any armed soldiers there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, in 30 seconds I'm going to check those texts to see if we are talking about the same thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you please would do that during the break, then you have an opportunity to put this additional question immediately after the break. We will consider what would be the order of questioning after the break, and then of course the Prosecution will have the opportunity to play the videotape. We will have a break until 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I apologise for resuming a bit later than we indicated but the Chamber thought it wise to look at the transcript as well, which we just received during the break. And in order to avoid any misunderstanding, I would just like to check with the Defence whether the lines they would like to confront the witness with, who is not yet in the courtroom, are the following lines: It's immediately -- I have got it in my transcript on page 63 at 18.02.46. The transcript as it is now, reads as following: Immediately after the problems with the -- technical problems with the video, I read: "Doctor, could I ask you that during the time that we have been talking about, from late 1992 through to the middle of 1994, was there any military presence in the state hospital? By that, I mean the presence of any armed soldier." The answer was "No." Question, "Was the -- " Then the answer continues: "In the hospital there was never any armed soldier present. The soldiers that came to the hospital on any basis, whether they were injured and wounded or needing medical aid and assistance or whether they came to visit somebody who was sick in hospital would always leave their weapons outside the hospital complex in a separate room designated for that." That's the lines we've spotted, and I see that there are several other lines which deal with the JNA leaving the hospital. So that's what we could find. So could you please clarify, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, whether this is the place you were talking about earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President, thank you. Most certainly, in that passage. We have some problems in finding the lines in the system, but we'll get better at it certainly. We are, indeed, speaking about this answer. The witness declared there had never been during the period 1992, 1994 armed personnel within the hospital.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As far as I remember, the question put to the witness where he was confronted with at least a possible contradiction was about another period of time, so I don't know whether it's of any use to put this question again to the witness. But I leave that up to the Defence. Then apart from that, the Chamber has considered whether the Defence will have a possibility for questioning the witness on the issue of the video. You have within the same time limits as the Prosecution will use, the possibility of questioning the witness on the video and strictly limited on the video. And I also can announce to you that this Chamber will take the Christmas recess to think over more thoroughly again the old question, I may say, the old question of whether the cross-examination will have to stay within the limits of the examination-in-chief, which is a rather difficult question. But it's just to announce. If you perhaps would find that some training today would be good, then I'm not opposing against it. Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Indeed, I had in mind that I would rise to my feet at the conclusion of this witness's evidence to raise that issue and to respectfully suggest that it be dealt with when the Trial Chamber resumes in January. But at this stage to point out that already the Prosecution has some problems as a result of that order and recommendation. On the 16th of November, the Pre-Trial Judge ordered that the Prosecution case be limited to 280 hours, and that period of time includes cross-examination, re-examination, and the Prosecutor's opening. 280 hours is approximately the time the Prosecution had indicated to the Pre-Trial Chamber it would require for just evidence in chief, not for cross-examination. Mr. President, there's a second issue, if I could. His Honour goes on to make a recommendation that the cross-examination of a witness should not exceed the time of the examination-in-chief. If I may refer to this witness as an example of how that is operating, the estimate given by the Prosecution in its Rule 65 ter summary for this witness was one hour. That was amended in the material that was handed to the Trial Chamber last week to one and a half hours. I now have the times. Examination-in-chief of this witness took one hour and 26 minutes. Cross-examination has taken 1 hour and 55 minutes. In other words, already the Defence has gone outside that recommendation. My proposal is that any time limit on cross-examination is -- has an air of unreality about it. It may be appropriate in many circumstances that cross-examination take less than the time taken in chief, on other occasions that it take more than the time taken in chief. My respectful submission is that the relevant issue is that is relevance. And that should be the guiding principle rather than an artificial time limit. So, Mr. President, I respectfully suggest that when we reconvene in January, that this issue be revisited and reconsidered, and I anticipate that will be my primary submission. In the meantime, because the Trial Chamber, and certainly the Prosecution, is confined by the orders and is subject to the recommendation, it will be necessary for us to take some measures in relation to our next witness. In other words, we will take less time in chief than we otherwise would have, and we do that also in the context that this witness has given evidence of a similar nature. The next witness will also be a doctor from the state hospital, and where the same issues have been covered by this witness, we will not lead that evidence. And we will leave it until January to consider the issue as a whole. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I indicate to both parties that the mere fact that I came already as an announcement by the Chamber with our intention to review this question thoroughly, that it's of great concern to the Chamber. And we're a bit handicapped by the fact that the decision of the 16th of November of the Pre-Trial Judge, there's still an appeal pending. So that I wouldn't say binds our hands, but it makes us a bit -- makes us -- we are trying to proceed not too drastically as this appeal is still pending. But if we could, as I told you, even without giving a binding order at this moment, if we could try and do some training. Of course, the time, I have been noting down also what time examination-in-chief and cross-examination took. If you could try to see where we can come -- if we try to do our best today, then this might be helpful for the Chamber to Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. give any rulings in January as well. So in order not to lose any more time, could you please bring in the witness, Mr. Usher. Ms. Pilipovic, would there still be this one question to be asked?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mandilovic, you said that in the month of April, before the army -- the Yugoslav People's Army left the hospital, the hospital had been surrounded by the patriotic league or the Territorial Defence. Were there any troops within the hospital and armaments? You were there the whole month of April.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I have already said something about this, and I'll repeat. Sometime in mid-April, there came a smaller military contingent to the military hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I have to remind you that you did not mention it, either during the examination-in-chief or during the cross-examination. You just said that the patriotic league surrounded the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry about that. In mid-April, a not very large contingent of troops arrived at the hospital. I think there were about 10 or 15 of them, including two officers, one older and one younger.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us the names of those officers? That would be my last question.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the names of the officers or the soldiers. They took up the 12th floor. They spent their time there. They spent their nights there. And from that point, they observed the surroundings. That's what I know.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know, is that direct knowledge or indirect?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did you see them? Did you talk to them?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did, informally, without going into any details, I talked to them just as I would talk to anyone else.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: In the period of 1992, 1993, 1994, was there any weaponry around the hospital like mortars and other weapons?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't notice any around the hospital.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Blaxill.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: My learned friend referred to 1992 in its entirety, so she's outside the period. Could we make it precise as to which period of 1992 she is talking about, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Pilipovic, would you please be more specific as far as the year 1992 is concerned? And apart from that, your indication that the question would be the last one seems to be irrelevant. If you say it's the last question next time, I might say --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're right, Your Honour. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Your Honours, I note the answer, however, that has been given as I was rising, so I think it has become academic. So I would withdraw the objection at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So is there any further question to be put or was this your last question?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was my last question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Pilipovic. Now we are at a point where the Prosecution may show the video. I hope its of a technically better quality than last time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, we are indeed obliged for the opportunity to try and cover that unfortunate technical problem we had last time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Dr. Mandilovic, I am going to play, ask the Court system to play to you a videotape, one where you will recall we had some technical problems last time we tried to play it. I'd like you, please, to take a close look at that video as it's played and I will have just one or two questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Could we now please play the videoclip in question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Thank you. I wonder now, please, if we can go back to the beginning and just freeze the first picture image from that clip. Yes, if you hold it frozen there, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Doctor, do you recognise that building?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. That's the state hospital in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And can you tell us, please, which facade of the state hospital that is? In other words, which direction does it face, north, south, east, or west?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This side faces south.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And can you, judging by the condition of the front of that building, give any indication as to when, perhaps, that image was filmed?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say for sure, but I can say with certainty that this shot was not taken in 1992. It must have been taken later.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Can you just tell us why you are able to make that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that in 1992, the damage to the facade and the building of the state hospital was not so extensive. The damage was inflicted progressively, so judging by the amount of damage, I believe this picture was taken after 1992. It's difficult to say precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Now, we saw a number of interior scenes in that short videoclip. Could you identify any of those interior shots and say whereabouts in the building they were?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can. I can identify these pictures very precisely because I worked in those areas, in those rooms. In particular, the shot that follows this shot of the facade is a room, women's cloakroom, which was used as a bandaging room for injured and wounded people. It had been vacated, and beds for the patients were put in. A few shots after that, we can see a scene with some of the wounded patients, and specifically two persons, a woman and a man, which were zoomed on by the camera. I also know the nurse who was shown passing by, and that woman worked in the hospital throughout the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Can you tell us on what floor or floors those interior scenes were taken?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the ground floor level, and the location was the ladies' cloakroom on the ground floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And in the building - let us use compass reference - was that towards the north side building, the south side, the east, or the west

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The ladies' cloakroom is on the ground floor in the north wing.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And Doctor, you say you recognised certainly two of the patients there. From that recognition, can you give us an indication as to when the scenes, including those patients, were shot or were filmed, I should say, sorry?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember these patients because I took part in a way in their treatment, or rather in their post-operative treatment. There were quite a lot of patients, but I happen to remember these particular ones because one of the specific features of them, they were a young boy and young girl. They were boyfriend and girlfriend who had been wounded at the same time, and they had serious injuries to their lower extremities, and they were brought in at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Can you say how old were those two people when they -- do you recall?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very young, about 20 years old.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And do you remember when it was that they were brought in to have their injuries treated?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was sometime in 1993, but I fear I won't be precise enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Doctor, we've seen other images in there of candles and of people at a sink and so forth. Can you say anything about the water and power supply at the time that that filming was done? What were the conditions in the hospital for that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this footage shows the actual state of affairs governing the working conditions in the hospital during the war. On the footage, and the clip, you can see something that I described earlier on, the lack of electricity, when we had to conduct complicated procedures by candlelight, and you can also see that there's no running water at the time. All the washing and rinsing had to be done with still water.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Dr. Mandilovic, thank you. There's just one other point I would like to address you on, and that is this: You have described an occasion when a shell hit the 11th floor when you were on that floor. Can you tell us, please, which side of the building that shell struck? Was it the north, southeast, or west?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The south, exclusively the south side.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: If I can refer you back to the frozen image on the video, which had gone -- I wonder whether that could be reinstated for just a moment. Examining that image, Dr. Mandilovic, can you, in fact, point out any damage to the building from that incident you described?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You can see it on the frozen image, the central part of the 11th floor, the middle of the 11th floor, when two patients' rooms were in fact damaged in the centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Can you tell us, of the number of floors shown in the image of the building, which one is the 11th floor? Perhaps you can count from the top down.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The last floor, top floor, is floor number 12, so the one immediately underneath that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: That concludes on that point. I'm obliged, again, to Your Honours for us being able to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Blaxill. Ms. Pilipovic, you have the opportunity now to cross-examine on this video and questions related to it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I should like to have the witness shown the frozen image again of the hospital. May we have that image shown again, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could the witness tell us where the Red Cross flag is on this building?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Red Cross flag, the big Red Cross flag, was in the first month's --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: With all due respect, there has been no mention of a Red Cross flag, and it is probably not even within the indictment period and it's not an issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, you mentioned a Red Cross flag, and as far as I remember no Red Cross flag has, until now, been mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I wanted to ask the witness where it was and within the frameworks of my cross-examination, just to point out where it was because we know that every hospital has its markings in wartime and that it always has a Red Cross emblem somewhere on the hospital. Now I just wanted to know where it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I apologise. One second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, the objection is sustained. Until now, there has been no mentioning in any way of a Red Cross sign on the hospital, and as I indicated before, questioning would be limited to the video shown and to questions asked concerning it. So you may proceed with another question.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown the footage with the nurse on the premises, please.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We've passed the image.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I understand that the nurse attended the operation.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not an operating theatre. It is the area where the patients were lying during their treatment. This was -- so it was just the bandaging stage, and the bandaging did not take place in the operating theatre but on the spot on the wards in the rooms, in the rooms you see on the footage.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown the footage again where we see that surgery is going on by candlelight, to explain to us what that is all about. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us the name of the doctor here that we see?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have to interpose. There was a reference made to surgery. I don't think at any time Dr. Mandilovic said this was a performance of surgery. This is some form of treatment, but not surgery, as I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please rephrase your question, if possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: On this image, can you identify the person -- the male person by the candle?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't. I can't give you his name and surname. But I think it was a physical therapist who was exercising the lower extremity, or in more specific terms, the foot of this patient.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: How can you see this in this footage?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you can see him exercising the foot. If you -- if the whole clipping is shown, then you'll see that this physical therapist is exercising the ankle joint.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know the name of the physical therapist?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm afraid I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown the image of the patients lying in hospital. There's one of a woman sitting down on a bed and talking to someone.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Is that the patient that you know, the boy and girl that you know?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's them. They were wounded together, and they were boyfriend and girlfriend, and that's why they have adjoining beds.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us their names?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm afraid I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When were they brought into hospital? What time was this, what period?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't be sure, but it must have been perhaps 1993. It's difficult to say. We had a lot of patients, and it was a long time ago. So I really can't be more specific.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: How often did you see them and contact them, because you say you remember them because you changed their bandages? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, among others, I changed their bandages, too. I dressed their wounds. Probably for about a month.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: How often did you dress their wounds during that month?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps once a day or every other day, depending on the needs and how much available staff there was.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did you talk to them during that month?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did they tell you where they had been wounded?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did, certainly. I think they said in the Marijin Dvor.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I apologise. I think we are now going beyond the time that we had discussed for the cross-examination on the issue of the video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Blaxill, I did write down that we started at least on the laptop at 11.24, we are now 11.31. That makes seven minutes that you started at 11.15 and you went on until 11.24. So that's nine minutes, so I think there are two minutes left for Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I stand corrected, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I would just like to have that frozen image again, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Where was the patients' card placed?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was on the side of the bed. We can't see it. On the railing of the bed, just cut off.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did you write in the time that you changed the bandages?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, actually, it's a temperature chart at the end of the bed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So what entries were made in that patients' card?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are two things. When we speak about the patient's administration, that's one thing, and then you have the temperature chart.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: What did it say on the case history?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the case history, the -- it would say what the injuries or wounds were and what surgical intervention was performed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Does the case history include anamnesis?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you take down the anamnesis on the basis of talks with the patient?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: What did it actually say in the anamnesis?

utterances.speaker: MILAN MANDILOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Pilipovic. Does the Prosecution want to put any additional questions, re-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Mr. President, no, we do not, and in fact the only thing I would now ask is if the videoclip could at this stage be marked for identification purposes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think, if you would not mind, I've got a whole list now of all kinds of things that went already through this courtroom, and one of them, the last number, is the videoclip concerning -- related to the testimony of Dr. Mandilovic. So I would rather go through that whole list at a later stage, but I have noted that you requested for marking for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One of my colleagues, any questions? No questions from the Bench. Then, Dr. Mandilovic, I would like to thank you very much for coming a very long way to The Hague, and I wish you a good journey home. Mr. Usher, could you please guide the witness out.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you, too, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Blaxill, and Mr. Ierace, who will be the next witness called by the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: It's Dr. Bakir Nakas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As soon as the usher has come back to the courtroom, I will ask him to bring the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Nakas. Can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. Yes, I can, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Rules require you to make a solemn declaration of which the text will be handed out to you, so I may invite you to make this declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Blaxill, I presume.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. THE COURT: You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Dr. Nakas, how are you, sir?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: Good morning. How do you do? I am fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Could you please give your full name for the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: My name is Bakir Nakas.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Date of birth, sir?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: I was born on the 26th of April, 1949.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Can you please tell us what your professional qualifications are.

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: I am a graduated physician, a specialist for infectious diseases, and for the past ten years, I have been performing the duties of an administrative person. Administrator, I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Where do you perform those duties of administration?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: Since the 10th of May, 1992, I have held the post as responsible administrator of the state hospital of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: The state hospital in Sarajevo, we've heard something about, Dr. Nakas. Can you tell me, sir, initially, when the conflict began in Sarajevo, was there any particular step you took to highlight the identity of state hospital as a medical facility?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence objects. My colleague said when the conflict began in Sarajevo. Could he specify which time he means? The witness has said nothing about that. And my learned colleague put the question himself as to when the conflict in Sarajevo began.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Blaxill, could you be more precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Yes, I'll be more precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Was there a time in 1992 when you took such a step in respect of your hospital?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: Officially speaking, on the 10th of May, the hospital was taken over by the legal authorities of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And up until then, it had been a military hospital in which, up until the 8th of April, I worked as a specialist doctor for infectious diseases. Upon arrival at the hospital again on the 10th of May, I was appointed administrator, hospital administrator, and in those first days, we undertook to visibly mark the building to show that it was a health institution. And this implied -- this implied raising a Red Cross emblem in a visible place on the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Whereabouts was that visible place and how large was this emblem?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: The hospital is located at Marijin Dvor, which is a district -- a central district of Sarajevo. And on several sides, it dominates the area. And the sign of the Red Cross was placed on the south side of the hospital, which was -- which faced directly towards Vrace hill and Trebevic. And from that location, the shells started flying. As for size, it was a standard type of flag which was no larger or smaller than the flag that is used for designating the state. Perhaps it was slightly longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Can you please say for how long that flag remained on the -- on the south side of the building?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: I think it remained there in the course of May, June, July, until September 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us, please, why it was then removed?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: As the flag was exposed to gunfire, it was all tattered, and that was the reason why we took it down.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: You have said that that side of the building faces towards Vrace hill and Trebevic, and you have made reference to "shells started flying." Could you please tell us how you determined?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the witness did not speak about Trebevic and Vrace. That was a question by my learned colleague, or perhaps I was not paying due attention. If we could go back and have a look at that part.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think about line 16, 17 of page 59, the answer included south side of the hospital which faced directly towards Vrace hill and Trebevic. And he says from that location, the shells started flying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic. Could you please --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I see it now, yes, on that page it does indeed say Vrace and Trebevic. Thank you

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I suggest that we first verify the basis of our objections and only then put them. You may proceed, Mr. Blaxill.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Dr. Nakas, I was going to ask you in what way did you make the conclusion that you stated from that location the shells started flying. On what evidence did you base that?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: I spent practically the entire month of March in the former military hospital as an active military person. And at the beginning of April, when it was possible to see certain firing positions from which the city of Sarajevo was targeted, it was possible to see this from the higher up floors of the central hospital building. And in my free time, on several occasions, I would go up there to those upper floors and look out towards the locations from which the shelling was coming and from which the shells fell on the city of Sarajevo. And one of those places was Vrace, Hresa, and the other surrounding hills around Sarajevo which can be seen from the hospital with the naked eye. The hospital itself, on the 13th of May, received a direct hit from Vrace, and in my personal assessment, it was a tank projectile. And after that, the sign was put up on the hospital building to show that it was a health institution.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Could you tell anything else from looking at the actual structure of your hospital that helped you in making a determination as to the source of fire?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: As I have already said, as the hospital building is the dominant building in this part of town in addition to several other buildings, the two UNIS buildings of the UNIS corporation, and the former government building of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the entire circle of 360 degrees, you could use to position and to look at the positions of the hills surrounding Sarajevo, which means that a visible distance, you could make out Mount Igman, Trebevic, Hresa. But Hum was blocked from view on the Vogosca side so that that northerly part was not clearly visible. You could see the south side best, partially the eastern reaches and the western side, in part, as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: What about -- what could you tell, however, by just looking at the facade of the building and any of the holes you could see? Did that help tell you anything about the source and type of fire?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: Absolutely correct. The south side of the hospital was the most exposed to the fire, and almost 85 to 90 percent of hits were on that side of the hospital. A lesser number of hits came from the eastern side or direction, one from the north, and on the western side, I think there was not a single hit. I'm talking about the whole period, not only in the first months of 1992, but the rest of the time as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Dr. Nakas, if I can move on, please, to the period after -- in fact, the month of September of 1992. May I ask you about the effects of sniping activity in the vicinity of the hospital, and I had only one question really. Were there any occasions where patients or staff within the hospital were injured as a result of sniper fire, inside the hospital, that is?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: As I have said, the hospital is located at the centre of Marijin Dvor, and a part of it faces directly the Trscanska, the street which connects the Kranjceviceva Street with the Marsal Tito Street. That street was known for a while as the sniper alley. As for the developments and woundings in the hospital itself, I can say that in October 1992, my secretary, who was at the time standing between my office and her office in the doorway, sustained a wound from a large bullet fired from a weapon we call PAM, anti-aircraft machine-gun. And the following year, in 1993, several people were wounded inside the hospital building on the side which is in the direct vicinity of the Trscanska Street.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Was there any particular incident involving yourself in or about August 1993?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: In that same office in which my secretary worked, during one of the morning meetings with the management of the hospital, a bullet flew in, also the PAM calibre, from the right-hand side of my desk. It hit the wall behind my back, ricocheted against another wall on my left side, and passed between my head and the head of my colleague who was sitting opposite me, and landed in the corner of the room.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Were you able both in the incident with your secretary and the one you have just described to us, were you able to work out the origin of fire on those occasions? If so, how?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: Judging by the location of the first impact, one could conclude that the position from which both hits originated was the slope of the Trebevic, which was called Kranjcevicenva. It is linked directly to the Vrace hill. It's an extension of the Vrace hill when you are talking towards Trebevic. It was not possible to conclude anything judging by the hole on the window -- in the window pane because there were no window panes. The windows were covered by foil. But the location of the impact inside the room led us to conclude where the bullet originated from.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And who actually held those territories that you have just Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. referred to on Trebevic and Vrace hill?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: I was born and bred in Sarajevo, and I know the roads around the town and I know the sections which were taken over in March and April by the then-Yugoslav People's Army. I also had some partial - and I am emphasise partial - knowledge about units of the JNA and the activities taking place surrounding Trebevic and on Trebevic itself, where trenches were being dug and connecting trenches under the pretext that they were needed for a military drill.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: If I may move forward, too, in fact the time from September 1992 onwards, Doctor, can you tell us who actually held that territory of Vrace hill and of Trebevic at that time?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: Practically from the 2nd of May, the first day when the barricades were put up in Sarajevo in 1992, when the position was marked which would later become the separation line, that area was under the control of the Serbian population of that part of the town, and the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: But turning to the time after September of 1992, what was the name of the force or group that held Vrace and Trebevic? By what name did you know them?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: In that period, members of the units who were holding this area were members of what we thought of as the former JNA and the so-called Serbian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And what did you know those people as at the time, say, that the bullet came in your office, in August 1993? By what name did you know those forces to be called then?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: Most often it was the Serbian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Doctor, can you tell us, in the course of 1992, 1993, and into the first half of 1994, what did you observe as the mental and emotional effect that the shelling and the sniping in Sarajevo had on the population, from your own observations?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: As I am a doctor, and also a person who had opportunity to have first-hand experience of all that was happening in Sarajevo, and I had a lot of contact with other people, I observed that people were prone to fear, depression. Some of them were lost. And I also encountered one of the cases which were very remarkable; namely, on the 2nd of May [as interpreted] when my father suddenly died while he was buying his newspaper outside the kiosk, and I found him dead in the morgue early that afternoon. It was only 15 days later, after the funeral, that my mother tried on two occasions to slash her veins and commit suicide. And she was a person who until that time was completely normal, and I know this because she brought us up.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Doctor, sorry, if I may --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, excuse me. I think that there is a problem in the translation. I'm not quite sure. I thought I heard the 2nd of March, and not the 2nd of May as appeared in the transcript. So I should like to draw your attention to that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please indicate the line you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Page 65, line 5.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see. Could you please ask the witness again whether -- as it is in the transcript now, whether this is correct or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Dr. Nakas, we have a little confusion, the date you gave for the death of your father. Can you tell us again what that date was and what were the circumstances again briefly?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: Since you asked me about the mental health of the population in 1992, and not specifically from the date when I was appointed administrator at the hospital, I said that I had a fresh memory of the death of my father on the 2nd of March, 1992, and that the day when the barricades were put up, the first barricades were put up in the city of Sarajevo was very well remembered because the barricades marked the future position of the separation line.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I thank you for that, Doctor. Now, there's one other thing we would like to address, please, and that is a question of documentation. Can you please very briefly describe during the conflict, what were the methods of record keeping that you had at your hospital, how would a record be created and kept for a patient when they were admitted.

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: I think I mentioned in my statement that until the 10th of May, 1992, the hospital was a military hospital in which the entire administration and the protocols were identical to those of the overall administration prevailing in the medical corps of the Yugoslav People's Army. As the hospital had large stocks of records and archives of all the patients, the reports of specialists and referrals, and since I and the personnel who continued working in May 1992 at the hospital were mostly the former staff of the military hospital, the administration and the protocols were identical to the procedures that we had followed for the previous ten years, with the proviso that the so-called computer analysis procedures had been introduced for the purpose of later processing the central unit in Belgrade. Records were kept in offices, case histories were kept; discharge lists and all the accompanying specialists reports and referrals were identical to the form they had before 1992 with the --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Doctor, if I could just interrupt you, may we just take very briefly a kind of step-by-step procedure. What is done and by whom is it done when the patient first comes into the hospital as a wounded person during that period.

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: There existed infirmaries or outpatient clinics and the centre of emergency medical aid. This centre for emergency medical aid and all the offices had their admission protocols in which based on the patient's statement, a record was made of the date of admission, name, year of birth, diagnosis, treatment, plus a remark or a suggestion made to the patient as well as a note concerning insurance, that is, whether the patient in question had military-issued insurance or civilian insurance. If a patient was admitted --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. This covers all patients. Now, at that point, who would have made those kind of entries? Prior to the point of the full admission to hospital, who would have made those entries and what level of training did they have to do that process?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: They were called medical technicians or nurses who were trained for that job and had worked on that job before as staff of the military hospital. In certain cases, the doctor also made certain entries in the protocol if the case involved specific interventions on the patient. But the records, that is the protocols, were generally the responsibility of medical technicians.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And subsequent to the admission of a patient into hospital for some kind of treatment or surgery or whatever, what would then be the kind of record kept about that patient and who would be the one to keep that record and maintain it as they were being treated?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: As I said, there is an admission unit at the hospital where the main log is kept of the patients who were admitted as inpatients. In that unit, the patient would get a registration number under which he was admitted. In the hospital, a case history would be opened including more extensive details of the patient including his full address, a contact person in case of death, or in case the patient needed to be brought something. A record would be made also of his blood type, his RH factor, and this was done by medical technicians who entered administrative data. The case history was filled by the doctors who received the patient and it consisted of two parts: One of them was the interview or the anamnesis, that is to say, whatever data can be provided by the patient himself on his condition and disease, and the second part, the doctor's report. That is the doctor's findings in the case. In the same file as the case history, other documents such as the temperature chart, specialist reports and all the relevant data were also kept such as the surgery list, the anaesthesiologist’s list, and at the end of the treatment, an epicesis [phoen] would be issued and the discharge list detailing the treatment and the condition of the patient at discharge. That was done by the doctors who were dealing with a patient.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And after that, what is the procedure for keeping those records and can you say what authority or responsibility you personally have in respect of records of your hospital?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: After the patient was admitted, his case history would be sent to the ward in which he was treated. Upon completion of the treatment, case histories were placed in envelopes, and in the first months or the first years, in 1992 and 1993, they were kept in various departments.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you. I was just asking specifically about the archiving, the keeping of your records, and then what authority you have in your particular position in respect of those records.

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: After the patients were discharged, the case histories were placed in the archive, and it was the responsibility of the administrator to issue a copy of the report at the request of the patient or a third party within a period of 40 years. As far as I know, nothing has changed in the regulations governing archives to this day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Blaxill, would this be a proper moment to have a short break for 20 minutes?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So we'll have a break until 20 minutes until 1.00, and then we'll continue until a quarter to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I apologise for resuming a bit late. General Galic. Mr. Usher is bringing in the witness. Okay. Mr. Blaxill, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Dr. Nakas, just before the break, you stated it was the responsibility of the administrator to issue a copy of the report at the request of patients or third parties. In your present occupation, sir, and the one you've held for some years, what is your authority in that regard? Is that your responsibility?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: Yes. At the request of a third party, I am authorised to be able to issue a copy of the report being requested on behalf of the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this point I have a batch of documentation I would like to have handed, if I may, to the witness, if I could have the usher's assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I believe all appropriate copies have been distributed and they have been disclosed earlier to my learned friends either in the course of disclosure or indeed a fresh bundle for purposes of today's use anyway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you intend to tender them into evidence later on?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Mr. Blaxill, could you please provide the numbers of the documents that you will be using, please, for the record?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: They are on the list?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. You will see each batch is actually given a prosecution number label. So on the record I can say that the current bundles are P1601, P3369, and I think 69.1, which is a translation, 2794 and 2795, P2506, P2183, P2795, P3573, and I think a point 1 as well as a translation, and P2265. I believe that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Blaxill, if someone on your team can check whether the numbers are right in the transcript while you proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I'm obliged, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Dr. Nakas, could you look at the bundle of documents that you have been handed. Are you familiar with that bundle of documents?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: Yes, some of these documents are familiar. They are copies of findings or reports of original documents which are stored in the hospital. Others are photocopies of the originals such as the case histories or discharge sheet, and the specialist findings that were given the patient after an intervention of any kind was performed on them while they were at the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Are you, therefore, able to authenticate that they are true copies of records from your hospital in respect of the named patients?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: Yes, with the proviso that sometimes the copies are of original discharge letters and specialist findings which the patients have in their own possession. But the text that is included in those findings is also to be found in the hospital protocol book.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Doctor, if you could just look at the very top bundle. I believe the patient name is Taric. Can you indicate within the records relating to that person which shows, as it were, the history that is taken down? In other words, the information as to the alleged cause of injury and the initial diagnostic description. Can you just point out the document in that bundle, for instance, which would show where that is located in the papers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please indicate in what exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: It is P1601. For our translation purposes, it is P1601.1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Is there a document in that point bearing the signature of a Dr. Vuletic?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: Yes. It is on the front page of the case history form. It says Taric, father's name: Ermin, Elma, the date of birth, the address, the category of the person insured, and the diagnosis or rather the medical intervention, and indicating when the patient was discharged. It was signed by the department doctor and the head of the department.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And in this particular case, who was the department doctor and who was head of department?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: In this specific case, the head of the department surgery was primarius Dr. Abdulah Hakas, and the department physician was Dr. Ranko Vuletic.

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Dr. Nakas, where you have case histories written down in this nature, and there is a signature at the end of it of a doctor, would that Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. person have been the one who actually noted down the history from that patient?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: In this concrete case, the anamnesis and examination of the patient upon admission was conducted by Dr. Pandza, and you will find him on the next page of this copy. And on the following page, the page after that, the epicesis or conclusion was written by the department doctor, that is to say, Dr. Ranko Vuletic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Dr. Nakas, where there is a passage of information written down in one of these forms, and a signature follows it, is it the case that the author of that passage of information is the person who signed it, or could that have come from another source? In other words, would Dr. Pandza have written the piece under which you see his signature, would Dr. Vuletic have written the piece under which that signature appears?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: Yes. For this specific patient, the first person to make an entry was Dr. Pandza, and the conclusion and discharge was written by Dr. Ranko Vuletic. The normal procedure is, standard procedure, is that the doctors who are on duty when the patient is admitted have to make entries for all the documents, and the person on duty when the patient is being discharged, then that physician discharges the patient.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence has a slight problem of a technical nature. I am looking at Document P1601. It is the discharge sheet, and it says Taric, Elma. Could my colleagues help me. I am unable to identify the document where it says Dr. Pandza. What page of the document is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I can assist that under the Exhibit Number P1601, there are in fact four pieces of paper, essentially. Maybe five. There is the front sheet, there is then a further extract, then there is - I will pronounce this wrongly I'm sure - Istorija Bolesti, consisting of two pages, and then the third. I wonder if it would assist with the ERN numbers, which, in fact, run from 02116303 through to 6307. I wonder if that helps my learned friend.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should like to thank my learned colleague, but I've only got it now so that now I'm able to follow. The bundle given to the Defence only has the first two pages, and then after that it follows on with some other documents. So that's the problem. I only have the discharge sheet and the signature of Dr. Jasminka [phoen] for this particular patient. But now I will be able to follow with the numbers you have given me and the documents given by the secretariat. We won't have any problems in the future. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, if you will allow me as much as possible, the Defence would wish because of an absolute rule -- general rule, at least, a few minutes before or perhaps a few seconds hearing the documents to which reference is made, in particular, when they have never been listed before. Thank you in advance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Blaxill, I noticed that we have got a list with exhibit numbers on it, but we are now confronted with other exhibit numbers as well, which might be a surprise for the Prosecution -- for the Defence as well. I'm not quite sure whether you discussed this. And apart from that, as far as I can see, that also P2272 and P2272.1 have been handed out, although perhaps not mentioned, as Madam Registrar tells me, on the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Then my apologies for an omission on my part if I didn't read out that number to the record, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is the Defence enough prepared to proceed or -- could you perhaps tell us when exactly the Defence was provided with at least the numbers that would be used during this examination-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: That's a three-fold answer to that. Last week, they were given the basic list with the numbers listed for the exhibits that would compromise the documentation today. On Wednesday, I understand the documents, but not with the exhibit numbers, and then today the documents again with the exhibit numbers. That is my understanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But all the numbers -- because you mentioned a lot of numbers. I've got three numbers on my list: 3573, 2272, and 2265. Or have I missed -- is there a newer list which I do not know of, or are these the three numbers indicated on the list under the name of Bakir Nakas?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I would like to at some moment to check these numbers against the documentation, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, could we ask to have the numbers -- reference numbers, ERN reference numbers. It would be much simpler to issue them immediately, Mr. Blaxill, electronically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Blaxill, I really have some problems because a lot of exhibits with numbers other than on my list are handed out. The same is true for the Defence; they should at least be given some time to find their way through these new exhibits, because we are now discussing Exhibit P1601, that is not on my list, for example.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sure we could resolve this with a little time to look at the documentation. If I could just advise Your Honours today, the very purpose of this is simply an issue of authentication. As to contents and as to the application of any of these documents to other elements of evidence subsequently in the trial, clearly that is not a matter for today. We are simply dealing with authentication.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If it's just a matter of authenticity of the documents, I suggest that we proceed. But if the Defence has any problems with authenticity in a later stage, then of course they can come back to it because it goes a bit too quick perhaps for them -- for me as well. So you may proceed limited to this aspect.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Yes. The only thing I think I wanted to ask you now about any particular document that we were looking at is simply: Would the doctor who completed that note, would they just get the information direct from the patient? Would that be their own source for that little history?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I apologise really. Please excuse me. As I have already said, I have got a good part of my documents on computer. Can the Prosecution give ERN numbers for reference so that I can follow in my notes and not find myself in a disadvantaged position?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see on the original list, there are ERN numbers mentioned. And I -- well, of course I haven't got them. Have you got -- the ERN number is the one that's on top?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: The one I am talking about as this moment, Your Honour, yes. In the Bosnian language, it is 02116306 and 6307; in the English translation, 03033693695.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, you will find them -- in the top of the documents, you will find the number, as far as I can follow. Please proceed, Mr. Blaxill.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I have no further questions on this issue of authenticity, Your Honours. Thank you. I'm wondering at this point in time whether you wish to have them formally tendered or you wish to mark them for identification until we are happy that everybody has resolved any problems as regards numbering?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, do you proceed with the other documents as well for authentification at this moment, or what's your intention?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Essentially, Your Honour, I'm inviting that we could treat all these documents as authentic records of the hospital. That's all -- the authenticity of the bundle --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: -- as identified by Dr. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's the whole bundle, all the documents --.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I -- I'm asking the Defence better -- even if it were on a provisional basis, you could agree that these are copies of authentic hospital documents. And I'll give you an opportunity, of course, to challenge the authenticity of the documents at a later stage, but just for practical sake, could we proceed just presuming at this moment that these are authentic documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence must point to a certain problem regarding authenticity at this point. On several occasions during our meetings with our learned friends from the Prosecution, the Defence put forward the problem of authenticity of documents exchanged between the parties. You will notice that the Prosecution, in its pre-trial brief and that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think that there's a problem with our transcript in the screen. It might have a technical cause. It stops on one of my screens at 13.09.42, and that is on the other one 10.08.55. Can the problem be solved or -- I'm just looking desperately to the booth with the technicians.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On this score, Mr. President, I think a page is missing a bit higher. I think a page is missing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm afraid that as long as there is no transcript, we can't deal with any matter at this moment. So the only thing I'm discussing now with Madam Registrar is the technical problem. We have to wait for a technician who could solve the problem, and I'm told that he will be there very soon. This, of course, doesn't prevent the parties for looking for any missing pages and then report as soon as the hearing has restarted what their findings are. I'm told that the system is working again. I see on my screen that the technical problem came up after I had said "I see on the original list there are ERN numbers mentioned. And I, of course, I haven't got them. Have you got the ERN number, that one that's on top?" And Mr. Blaxill said, "The one I'm talking about ... in the Bosnian language is," and then he started giving a number. That's where we resume, Mr. Blaxill. So if you would finish what you were saying there, and everything has to be repeated on from that moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Yes. The ERN I see from these documents - I will read - 02116305. And then 6306 and 6307 refers to the exemplar document that we are actually discussing. In the translation, they are ER numbers 03033692, 93, 94, and 95.
